svg.aria-label: Wading across a river: don't cross unless you must; fast water about 15 cm deep can knock you over, and in knee-deep fast water you can barely stand. 1 Do not cross if: a stick thrown in floats faster than a brisk walk, the water in the fast part is above the knee, the water is murky and you cannot see the bottom, there are waterfalls, rapids, deep pools or fallen trees not far downstream, it has just rained heavily and the water is rising, or you are very tired or cold; if unsure, wait, or look along the bank for a better place, or go round. 2 Choose a wide stretch with a smooth surface and a bed of small pebbles, not a narrow stretch or the outside of a bend; don't walk on wet logs or jump across slippery rocks. 3 Alone: undo the pack's hip belt and chest strap, keep your shoes on, face upstream and shuffle sideways in small steps, with a trekking pole or stick planted on the upstream side for three points of contact, moving only one point at a time, heading diagonally downstream. 4 In a group: two or three people link arms or hold each other's packs, line up one behind another along the current and shuffle across, the strongest person upstream, with someone downstream ready to catch. 5 Swept away: shed your pack, lie on your back with your feet downstream near the surface, push off rocks with your feet, scull with your arms and swim diagonally to the bank; stand up only where the water is slow and shallow, do not try to stand in fast water, and do not grab fallen trees or branches. Never tie a rope to the person crossing
svg.title: Wading across a river: judge, choose a spot, cross, if swept away

g.text: Wading across a river: don't cross unless you must
Wading is a much-underestimated danger: once you are knocked over, your pack drags you under
① Can you cross? Do not cross if:
✗ Fast current: a stick thrown in floats faster than a brisk walk
✗ The water in the fast part is above the knee
✗ The water is murky and you can't see the bottom
✗ Waterfalls, rapids, deep pools or fallen trees not far downstream
✗ It has just rained heavily and the water is rising
✗ You are very tired or very cold
✓ If unsure, wait: a mountain stream swollen by rain often drops
again within a few hours; a river fed by melting snow and ice
usually carries less water in the morning than in the afternoon
✓ Or look along the bank for a better place, or go round
② Choosing where to cross (top view)
✗ Don't walk on wet logs or
✓ Smooth surface, bed of small pebbles
Face upstream and shuffle sideways in small
steps. Move only one point of contact at a
time; get steady before moving the next
④ Crossing as a group (top view)
Two or three people link arms or hold packs,
line up one behind another along the current
and shuffle across; post a catcher downstream
⑤ Swept away: on your back, feet downstream
scull with both arms to steer
Shed your pack first; stand up only where
the water is slow and shallow
✗ Don't try to stand and walk in fast water:
a foot can jam between rocks, and the
current pushes you over and holds you under
✗ Don't grab fallen trees or branches in the
water (you can be swept under them)
Swim to the bank at an angle to
the current, not straight against it
✗ Never tie a rope to the person crossing: if they are knocked over,
the rope holds them under water
To help a companion in the water: protect yourself first. From the bank, throw a rope or
something that floats, or hold out a branch or trekking pole. Without professional rescue
training, don't go into the water to rescue them.
